name: Wrenchy: Car Service Log
subtitle: Rego, Mileage & Oil Reminders
promotionalText: Your log book history stays on the phone. No account, no server, nothing to sync and lose. Every service, oil change and rego date in one log you keep.
description:
Your service records, kept for as long as you own the car. On your phone, not on someone else's server.

Most car maintenance apps want an account, a login and a sync. One broken login and years of log book history are gone. Wrenchy works differently: no account, no server, nothing to sync. Every oil change, tyre rotation and repair you log stays on your phone.

WHAT IT DOES
- Log oil changes, tyre rotations, brakes, filters, coolant, spark plugs and anything else you type in, on any number of cars
- Know when the next one is due, by date or by kilometres, whichever comes first, with a reminder on the day
- See the full service history for each car at a glance
- Export the lot to CSV whenever you want. Export is free for everyone and never behind the subscription

WHY IT'S DIFFERENT
No account. No login. No server. No sync to break. Your history cannot vanish, because there is nothing for it to vanish from. It sits on the phone, the same way the paper log book sits in the glovebox.

BUILT FOR THE WAY WE DRIVE HERE
- Kilometres, not miles. Due dates read off the odometer the way the log book is stamped
- Log book servicing on your car's own intervals, whether the book says 10,000 km, 15,000 km or twelve months
- Rego and the roadworthy sit in the same log as the servicing. What the safety check is called and how often it comes around is set by your state, or by the WoF cycle in New Zealand, so you set the date and Wrenchy reminds you
- Dark, glare-friendly screens, built to be read in the driveway or standing at the workshop counter

WHO IT'S FOR
Daily drivers, weekend mechanics, tradies keeping a ute on the road, and anyone who wants proof of service history when the car goes up for sale. A private buyer discounts what you cannot show them, and so does the dealer taking it as a trade-in. Keep every oil change, tyre and repair in one searchable log instead of a folder of receipts in the glovebox.

Free for one car. Wrenchy Pro adds unlimited cars and custom service intervals. Export always stays free, for everyone.

notes.inspectionTerm: Roadworthy (rego alongside it; WoF acknowledged for New Zealand readers)
notes.reasoning: Australia searches in its own words, so the indexed fields are built from them rather than from the US field. The name takes the three highest-volume generic tokens in the harvest (car, service, log), which between them cover 'car service', 'car services log', 'car service book' and 'car log book'. The subtitle spends its 30 characters on words the name does not have: 'rego' is the single most Australian query in the harvest and no global competitor targets it, 'mileage' and 'oil' plus 'reminders' pick up the two biggest remaining seeds ('mileage tracker', 'oil change reminder'). Keywords then hold only unused tokens - maintenance, tracker, vehicle, logbook, book, tyre (never 'tire'), change, odometer, km, history, mechanic, roadworthy, repair - with no word repeated from name or subtitle. Deliberately left out: the whole 'car expenses' seed cluster, which is the second-largest group in the harvest but describes cost tracking Wrenchy does not do; the word 'australia', which several harvest rows carry but which is dead weight inside the AU storefront's own index; and every competitor app name. The description is metric throughout, calls periodic servicing a log book service and the workshop a workshop, matching the in-app en-AU overlay, and names the statutory check 'roadworthy' - the only word that reads nationally - while explicitly saying the cadence is set by your state or by the New Zealand WoF cycle, so nothing here promises one national test. What the harvest could not tell me and is judgement: the relative volume of 'logbook' as one word versus 'log book' as two (both spellings appear, so the name carries 'log' and the keyword field carries 'logbook' and 'book' separately), and whether 'roadworthy' pulls enough search volume to justify its ten characters - it is kept because it is low competition and consistent with the app's own wording.
